top.line: Selling less code: the economics of customised open source
top.para: We sell customised versions of open source software, relicensed to one customer. The value is less complexity: the customer pays for the features they use and stops carrying the rest. Open source makes it possible, the maker certifies it, the pipeline gets paid for, and our stack signs, enforces and insures each build.

in-short.line: Seven lines from the model to the price
in-short.para: Customised, relicensed versions; the product is less complexity; every feature has a cost; open source makes it possible; the pipeline is tied to revenue; each build is signed with a smaller policy; more customisation costs more.

buying.line: What the customer is really buying
buying.para: Branding is the least of it. A customer who needs 10% of the features should not pay for, maintain, learn or be exposed by the other 90%. Our earlier arguments for running less code left open who pays for the removal; the customer does, because it is what they buy.

moving-parts.para: The best way to avoid a vulnerability is to have less code; when the next flaw lands, a customised version is more often unaffected. We are happy to own less: the base stays open and maintained by many, and we own the fit.

open.line: Why open source makes it possible
open.para: With the code, agents can build analysis, environments and a knowledge graph of what one customer uses, so code can be removed safely; and the maker, who understands and invested in it, is best placed to certify the result.

loop.line: The loop: the pipeline gets paid for
loop.para: When customising is the maker's cost, the maker designs for mix and match and invests in CI, tests, non-functional requirements, threat models and certification, which usually fight for budget because they are not tied to revenue. Usage data becomes a revenue question.

maker.line: The maker should do the customising
maker.para: The maker has the expertise, so it is cheapest for them: we customise our own stack, and pay other makers to customise theirs, or do not do it.

stack.line: How it fits RiskMandate, sgit and SHarness
stack.para: An open base; a customised build versioned in an sgit vault with a hash; a licence signed with our key over that hash; a smaller behaviour policy enforced by SHarness; and fewer rows for RiskMandate's insurers to price.

price.para: The more customisation, the higher the price, which rewards keeping code open and shared; everything we make is open source, and what we sell is the fit, the certification and the licence.

limits.para: A model, not yet a business at scale; the percentages are illustrations; removal needs maps and tests and upkeep; relicensing depends on the base's licence; I build the stack it argues for.

sources.para: My memo of 30 October 2026 and the earlier articles on less code, maintenance, certification, CI and insurance.
